messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Avoid Sex: Sex, Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
Malia was 19 when she first came for help, a young woman from an Oceanian background who had grown up around the sea and now worked as a fisherman in the same coastal community where she had always lived. Before the event, she had been known as steady and hardworking, someone who could get up before dawn and spend long hours on the water without complaint. That changed after she witnessed a violent incident in her village one evening when she was still younger, an event she describes only in fragments because the details do not come to her as a complete picture. What stays with her is the force of it: the sound of rushed movement, footsteps coming quickly behind and nearby, and other related sounds that now feel loaded with danger in a way they did not before. She remembers the sudden surge in her body before she could think, the jolt of being thrown into alertness, and then the horrible sense that something terrible was unfolding in front of her and that she had not been able to stop it. When she recalls it now, she often does not see a clear image at all; instead she is overtaken by the same emotional intensity, as if the fear and helplessness arrive full strength without a visual memory to contain them. At other times, the memory forces its way in when she is not wanting it, interrupting ordinary moments with a rush of guilt. She has come to believe that she should have protected others and failed, and this belief still lands on her with particular force when she thinks back on what happened.

Since then, Malia has found herself scanning for danger in ways that feel immediate and bodily. She says her body reacts before her mind has time to catch up, and that she often knows she is frightened only after her muscles have already tightened and her chest has already gone tense. She becomes especially unsettled when something takes longer than expected, because the delay itself makes her assume that something bad is happening. On the fishing boat, if a crew member is late returning with gear or if a routine task takes longer than usual, she finds herself watching the horizon and looking around with growing unease, certain that the delay means trouble. The same kind of reaction happens on land. A bicycle passing close by can make her freeze or jerk away, not because the bicycle itself is dangerous, but because it carries the same sense of sudden approach that now feels threatening. Footsteps behind or near her are particularly difficult; if she hears them on the road, in a yard, or near the dock, she becomes tense and checks who is there. Related sounds can have a similar effect, enough that she has begun to notice how quickly her body prepares for danger before she has decided what she is reacting to.

In the months after the event, Malia tried to keep herself busy. She began working excessively, taking on more hours whenever she could so she would not be alone with her thoughts. The long shifts on the water and around the boats gave her structure and kept her from sitting still with the memories, but they also left her exhausted. Outside of work, she increasingly spent long hours on her phone, games, or the internet, scrolling until late because being absorbed in the screen felt easier than being left alone with what came up in silence. This has affected her relationship as well. She avoids sex, and she does not describe this as lack of interest so much as a wish to keep distance from experiences that make her feel too exposed and too aware of her own body. She has been embarrassed by how difficult it has become to feel at ease even with someone she cares about, and she worries that her partner does not fully understand why she pulls away.

What troubles Malia most is the conviction that she is somehow unsafe in her own body. She says it feels as though her body keeps reacting as if she is still in danger even when she knows, rationally, that she is not. That disconnect leaves her frustrated and ashamed, especially when the reaction is immediate and seems to happen without permission. She also fears what her own anger might become. In quieter moments she worries, with a seriousness that frightens her, that she will not be able to control her anger and will do something terrible. She does not describe acting on this fear, but the fear itself has become a prominent part of how she monitors herself, as if she must constantly watch for any sign that she might lose control.

By the time she sought treatment, Malia had reached a point where the effort of managing her days had become too heavy to keep carrying alone. The triggers were showing up too often in ordinary life, her concentration was slipping at work, and the constant push to stay busy was no longer enough to keep the memories out. She came hoping for some relief from the sudden floods of guilt and fear, and with a guarded wish that she might one day move through her work, her relationship, and the spaces of her daily life without feeling braced for danger at every delayed step or nearby footfall.
